theme: Itchy skin & the YouTube boom · 가려움의 과학과 유튜브의 힘

tracks.title: Why do we itch?
tracks.note: 우리는 왜 가렵고, 왜 남이 긁는 걸 보면 나도 가려워질까요? 피부·기생충(parasite) 얘기가 나와서 임상 쪽 단어 복습에도 좋아요. 1회차는 대략적인 내용만, 2회차는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Hello and welcome to 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: I'm Neil.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: And I'm Georgie.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Find the vocabulary, definitions and a free worksheet on our website, bbclearningenglish.com.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: So, Georgie we're going to talk about something a little different today.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: We're talking about itching.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Now an itch is that unpleasant feeling you get on your skin that you have to scratch with your fingers.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: What sort of things make you itch?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, funny you should ask, because I'm actually wearing quite an itchy jumper at the moment and it's making me want to scratch my skin.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: What about you?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, recently I was bitten by a mosquito and, as you know, when you get bitten by a mosquito, it's really itchy.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: I had to scratch loads and loads.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Oh, I hate it when that happens.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: It was horrible.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: In this podcast, we're going to hear from some experts about why we itch and how scratching can be good for us.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: And as usual, we'll be learning some useful new vocabulary.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, we're going to start with a quiz question of course, Georgie.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: It's a bit of a different one today.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Dr Henning Holle studies the psychology of itching, and he played some scratching sounds to the guests on the BBC World Service programme CrowdScience.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Now the question is, what is being scratched?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: You have three choices: a) an arm, b) a beard, or c) some jeans.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, let's listen...

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, that sounded a bit hairy, so I'm going to go with b) a beard.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, we'll find out at the end of the programme.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So, Neil, I mentioned that my jumper was a bit itchy but sometimes I feel itchy for no particular reason.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So, what's going on there?

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, that's something that the listeners of BBC World Service programme CrowdScience also wondered.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: They wanted to know the answer to that.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: The presenter, Anand Jagatia, spoke to itching expert Sonja Ständer to find out more.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Let's listen.

transcript.speaker: Anand Jagatia
transcript.text: There's lots of science to unpack here.

transcript.speaker: Anand Jagatia
transcript.text: Sonja, what actually is itchiness?

transcript.speaker: Sonja Ständer
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Sonja Ständer
transcript.text: So, by scratching the skin, we remove parasites or plants or anything that does not belong on the skin.

transcript.speaker: Sonja Ständer
transcript.text: And so, we start to scratch at the very same area where we itch and remove it.

transcript.speaker: Sonja Ständer
transcript.text: And it can no longer damage the skin and harm ourselves.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Anand says there's a lot of science to unpack about itchiness.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Unpack here means explain.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Sonja explains that when our skin feels itchy, we scratch it, and that helps to get rid of parasites and other harmful things on our skin.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Parasites are animals or plants that live on another animal and feed from them.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So, Neil, itching is our skin's way of protecting itself against harmful parasites.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: And I have to say, all of this talk of itching and scratching is making me feel a bit itchy right now.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, that's interesting because Dr Henning Holle wanted to study whether just thinking about itching makes us more likely to feel itchy.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Henning and his team studied what happened when people watched videos of itching and scratching.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Let's listen to him speaking to BBC World Service programme CrowdScience.

transcript.speaker: Dr Henning Holle
transcript.text: And what we found in this study was, yes, these scratching videos indeed made people feel itchier.

transcript.speaker: Dr Henning Holle
transcript.text: They also started to scratch themselves more spontaneously.

transcript.speaker: Dr Henning Holle
transcript.text: So, the answer is basically yes, you can catch a scratch.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: In Henning's study, when people watched videos of scratching, they scratched themselves spontaneously.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: If you do something spontaneously, you do it without being asked or without thinking.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So, Henning concludes that yes, you can catch a scratch, just like you might catch an illness.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Catch in this context means get from someone else.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Georgie, I think it's time for the answer to my quiz question.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: We had a clip of people scratching and you had to decide what is being scratched.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: I said that was a beard.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Well, let's see if the people who are listening to this on the programme CrowdScience agreed.

transcript.speaker: Sonja Ständer
transcript.text: It sounds like hairy skin so I would go for the scalp.

transcript.speaker: Anand Jagatia
transcript.text: Yeah, I think it's beard or something because it does sound like there's hair there.

transcript.speaker: Dr Henning Holle
transcript.text: It is definitely hairy skin and Anand was spot on.

transcript.speaker: Dr Henning Holle
transcript.text: So, it is indeed a beard scratch that we were listening to.

transcript.speaker: Anand Jagatia
transcript.text: Wow!

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So I was right!

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: You were.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Congratulations!

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Let's recap the vocabulary we learned in this programme, starting with itch, which is an unpleasant feeling on your skin.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: And something can be described using the adjective itchy.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: When you feel an itch, you often scratch it with your fingers by rubbing your nails on the skin.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: If you unpack an idea or scientific concept, you explain it in clear detail.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: A parasite is an animal or plant that lives on another animal and feeds on it.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: If you do something spontaneously, you do it without being asked or without thinking.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Catch can be used to mean get from someone else, such as an illness.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: For example, you can catch a cold.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Once again, our six minutes are up, but you can test what you've learned with the worksheet on our website, bbclearningenglish.com.

transcript.speaker: Neil
transcript.text: Thank you for joining us and goodbye.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Goodbye.

listening.task: 6 Minute English를 한 번은 대략적인 내용만 듣고, 두 번째는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요. 그다음 퀴즈에 답해 보세요. 'unpack'과 'spontaneously'가 나오는 부분을 잘 들어 보세요.

quiz.q: Dr Henning Holle played a scratching sound. What was being scratched? a) an arm, b) a beard, c) some jeans
quiz.answer: b) a beard (수염). 보너스: 긁는 영상을 보기만 해도 사람들이 더 가려워하고 저절로(spontaneously) 긁기 시작했대요. 'You can catch a scratch!'

sentences.text: Now an itch is that unpleasant feeling you get on your skin that you have to scratch with your fingers.
sentences.ko: 가려움(itch)은 피부에 느껴지는, 손가락으로 긁어야만 하는 불쾌한 느낌이에요.

sentences.text: So, by scratching the skin, we remove parasites or plants or anything that does not belong on the skin.
sentences.ko: 피부를 긁어서 우리는 기생충이나 식물, 피부에 있으면 안 되는 것들을 없애요.

sentences.text: So, Neil, itching is our skin's way of protecting itself against harmful parasites.
sentences.ko: 그러니까 가려움은 해로운 기생충으로부터 피부가 스스로를 지키는 방법이네요.

sentences.text: And what we found in this study was, yes, these scratching videos indeed made people feel itchier.
sentences.ko: 이 연구에서 우리가 발견한 건, 네, 긁는 영상이 실제로 사람들을 더 가렵게 만들었다는 거예요.

sentences.text: If you do something spontaneously, you do it without being asked or without thinking.
sentences.ko: 어떤 일을 spontaneously(자발적으로/무심코) 한다는 건, 누가 시키지 않아도 또는 생각 없이 한다는 뜻이에요.

reading.title: YouTube’s dominance has Hollywood running scared
reading.summaryKo: 유튜브가 미국 TV 시청 시간의 15.8%를 차지하며 넷플릭스·디즈니·파라마운트·워너를 합친 것과 맞먹게 됐어요. 2025년 매출 600억 달러로 넷플릭스(450억)를 넘었고, 선불 없이 광고 수익을 나누는 저위험 모델과 AI 도구로 크리에이터를 키워요. 할리우드는 숏폼 도입, 크리에이터·임원 영입으로 반격하지만 아직은 유튜브가 한참 앞서 있다는 내용이에요. (공개 전재본 기준 발췌)
excerpt: YouTube’s effect on the media zeitgeist has been palpable this year. ... Nielsen, a data gatherer, measured YouTube’s share of America’s TV watching at 15.8% in August, almost as much as Netflix and the streaming services of Disney, Paramount and Warner Bros combined. That is double its level in early 2023, when YouTube overtook Netflix as the biggest streamer.

YouTube benefits from a business model that has less risk than that of its rivals. Whereas studios and streamers pay upfront to commission content, and own or license the resulting work, YouTube usually pays nothing in advance. Instead it takes a 45-55% cut of ad revenue and channel subscriptions.
reading.tip: Economist 스타일: 'Whereas A ..., B ...' 대조 구문을 찾아보세요. 숫자(15.8%, $60bn, 45-55%)에 동그라미 치면서 읽으면 구조가 빨리 잡혀요.

vocab.example: There's lots of science to unpack here.
They started to scratch themselves spontaneously.
YouTube's effect on the media has been palpable this year.
Studios pay upfront to commission content.
YouTube takes a 45-55% cut of ad revenue.
Netflix is trying to poach YouTube creators.

writing.prompt: How do you and your family use YouTube? Write 3–5 sentences in English. Is it more useful or more of a time-killer for you?
writing.question: Would you rather watch a YouTube creator or a Netflix show tonight, and why?
writing.hint: 이런 표현을 써 보세요: I usually watch ... on YouTube. / My kids love ... / Whereas Netflix ..., YouTube ... / For me, it's mostly a way of killing time / learning ...

speaking.prompt: In one minute, explain to a coworker why we feel itchy and why watching someone scratch can make you itch too.
phrases: Itching is the skin's way of protecting itself.
Scratching helps get rid of parasites.
You can actually catch a scratch, like catching a cold.
speaking.alt: 쉬운 버전: What YouTube channel do you watch the most? Tell me about it in three sentences.

evening.note: 수요일, 한 주의 가운데예요. 어제 이어서 10페이지. 피곤하면 5페이지만 읽어도 충분해요. Minimum day도 OK.
